subject: PE
overview: Lifetime Fitness runs 45 minutes a day and alternates short classroom concepts (training science, nutrition, safety) with real workouts the student logs. Demonstrate each skill, have the student practice while you watch with the week's cues, then let them perform and record data; safety and correct form come before intensity. Keep all fitness data in one journal so the baseline, midyear, and final tests can be compared and used for the personal plan.

weeks.prep: Gather a measuring tape, stopwatch, sit-and-reach box (or a yardstick taped to a box), cones, and a notebook to serve as the fitness journal. Measure a flat 1-mile route (4 laps of a standard track) and look up current Fitnessgram Healthy Fitness Zone (HFZ) charts for your student's age and sex on the CDE site. Have the student wear athletic shoes and bring water.
misconceptions: Thinking a low score is a 'fail.' Explain that a baseline is just a starting point; the goal is personal improvement and reaching the Healthy Fitness Zone.
Rushing push-ups or curl-ups to get a higher count. Fitnessgram uses a cadence (1 rep every 3 seconds); reps that break form or cadence do not count.
Bouncing in the sit-and-reach. Only a slow, held reach (1 second) counts; bouncing risks strain and inflates scores.

days.guide: Introduce the five health-related fitness components (cardiorespiratory endurance, muscular strength, muscular endurance, flexibility, body composition). Have the student take resting heart rate for 60 seconds at the wrist or neck, warm up 5 minutes, then walk/run the measured mile while you time it. Record time and how they felt (RPE 1–10) in the journal.

questions.q: Name the five health-related components of fitness.
questions.a: Cardiorespiratory (aerobic) endurance, muscular strength, muscular endurance, flexibility, and body composition.

questions.q: Where can you find your pulse, and why count for a full 60 seconds at rest?
questions.a: At the radial artery (thumb side of the wrist) or carotid artery (side of the neck, press gently). A full minute at rest gives a more accurate count than a short sample.

days.guide: Demonstrate a curl-up (knees bent ~140°, feet flat, hands slide across a 3-inch strip) and a 90° push-up (elbows bend to 90°, body straight). Play or tap a cadence of one rep every 3 seconds; the test stops at the second form correction or when cadence is broken. Record both counts.

questions.q: What is the Fitnessgram cadence for curl-ups and push-ups?
questions.a: One repetition every 3 seconds (20 per minute).

questions.q: What does the 90° push-up test measure?
questions.a: Upper-body muscular strength and endurance.

days.guide: Model the back-saver sit-and-reach: one leg straight against the box, other knee bent with foot flat, reach forward slowly four times and hold the fourth for 1 second; test each side. Then the trunk lift: lie face down and lift the upper body slowly, hold, and measure chin height (max 12 in counted). Practice once before recording.

questions.q: Why is the sit-and-reach done one leg at a time ('back-saver')?
questions.a: Bending one knee reduces strain on the lower back while still measuring hamstring flexibility of the straight leg.

questions.q: In the trunk lift, why is the score capped at 12 inches?
questions.a: Lifting higher than 12 inches can hyperextend and stress the lower back; it adds no health benefit.

days.guide: Measure waist circumference at the navel and height in the same units; compute waist ÷ height. Explain that a ratio under about 0.5 is generally considered healthy and that this is a screening tool, not a judgment. Set up a 7-day activity log (minutes, type, intensity) using a phone or pedometer.

questions.q: A student's waist is 30 in and height is 66 in. What is the waist-to-height ratio, and is it under 0.5?
questions.a: 30 ÷ 66 ≈ 0.45, which is under 0.5 (the general healthy guideline).

questions.q: How many minutes of activity per day do guidelines recommend for teens?
questions.a: At least 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity daily, including vigorous, muscle-strengthening, and bone-strengthening activity at least 3 days per week.

days.guide: Help the student look up the HFZ chart for their age/sex and mark each result as 'in HFZ' or 'needs improvement.' They write three findings in the journal (one strength, one need, one surprise). Check that each finding cites an actual number.

questions.q: What does 'Healthy Fitness Zone' mean?
questions.a: A Fitnessgram criterion score that indicates a level of fitness associated with good health for that age and sex — it is a health standard, not a ranking against others.

questions.q: Which fitness component does the 1-mile run mainly measure?
questions.a: Aerobic capacity (cardiorespiratory endurance).

weeks.assessment_key: Baseline fitness profile rubric (4 levels). 4 – All tests completed with correct technique; every result recorded with units, compared with the correct HFZ, and three findings each cite data. 3 (proficient) – All tests recorded and compared with HFZ; findings reference results. 2 – Some tests missing or HFZ comparison incomplete. 1 – Data mostly missing or unlabeled.

weeks.prep: Print or draw a goal sheet (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound) and a FITT planning grid. Have a jump rope, fitness journal, and a safe walking/jogging route. Review the student's week 1 baseline data so goals can be built from it.
misconceptions: Writing vague goals like 'get fit.' Push for a number and date: 'Improve my mile from 10:30 to 9:45 by December 1 by running 3x/week.'
Confusing overload with doing as much as possible. Overload means slightly more than the body is used to, increased gradually (progression).
Believing gains are permanent. Reversibility: fitness declines when training stops, so consistency matters.

days.guide: Explain each letter of SMART with an example. The student writes two goals based on baseline weaknesses, then completes a 20-minute circuit (e.g., 1 min jump rope, 15 squats, 30-sec plank, repeat). Check that each goal has a number and a deadline.

questions.q: Rewrite 'I want to be stronger' as a SMART goal.
questions.a: Example: 'I will increase my 90° push-ups from 12 to 20 by March 1 by doing push-up workouts 3 days a week.' (Must be specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and dated.)

days.guide: Teach FITT: Frequency (how often), Intensity (how hard), Time (how long), Type (what activity). The student fills in a FITT grid for one goal, then walks/jogs 25 minutes. Check that intensity is measurable (heart rate zone or RPE).

questions.q: Write a FITT plan for improving aerobic endurance.
questions.a: Example: F = 3–5 days/week; I = 60–80% heart rate reserve or RPE 5–7; T = 20–40 min; T = jogging, cycling, or swimming.

questions.q: Which FITT letter changes if you go from walking to jogging at the same time and frequency?
questions.a: Intensity (and arguably type) — jogging is a higher intensity.

days.guide: Define overload, progression, specificity, and reversibility with examples. Do an interval walk/jog (e.g., 2 min jog/1 min walk ×7). Afterwards ask the student to name which principle the interval session applies.

questions.q: A swimmer wants to run faster but only trains in the pool. Which principle is violated?
questions.a: Specificity — training should match the desired outcome; to improve running, you must run.

questions.q: What does reversibility mean?
questions.a: Fitness gains are lost when training stops ('use it or lose it').

days.guide: Brainstorm barriers (time, weather, motivation, cost, safety) and match each with a strategy (schedule it, indoor workout, workout partner, free resources). Then complete a 30-minute bike ride or hike and log it.

questions.q: Give one barrier to activity and a practical strategy to overcome it.
questions.a: Example: 'No time' → schedule three 20-minute sessions in the calendar before school; 'bad weather' → indoor bodyweight circuit or online workout video.

days.guide: Review the goal sheet and FITT plan with the student against the rubric; ask them to explain how they'll measure progress. They complete and log a 30-minute activity of their choice.

questions.q: How will you know if your SMART goal is met?
questions.a: By retesting the measurable outcome (e.g., push-up count or mile time) by the stated deadline and comparing to baseline.

weeks.assessment_key: Goal sheet and FITT plan rubric. 4 – Two SMART goals with all five elements based on baseline data; FITT plan specifies measurable frequency, intensity (HR zone/RPE), time, and type, and applies overload/progression. 3 (proficient) – Two SMART goals with numbers and dates; complete FITT plan. 2 – Goals missing measurable or time element or FITT incomplete. 1 – Vague goals, no FITT plan.

weeks.prep: Set out cones for a 20-m warm-up lane; have water bottles ready. Read the CDC heat illness signs (heat exhaustion vs. heat stroke) so you can teach them confidently. Plan to run the fartlek day in a shaded area or early morning.
misconceptions: Doing long static stretches before vigorous activity as a warm-up. Dynamic movement raises muscle temperature better; save long static holds for the cool-down.
Waiting until thirsty to drink. Drink before, during, and after activity, especially in heat.
Thinking heat stroke victims always sweat a lot. Heat stroke may involve hot skin and confusion (sweating may stop); it is a 911 emergency.

days.guide: Lead the student through a 10-minute dynamic warm-up down and back the cone lane: easy jog, leg swings, walking lunges, high knees, butt kicks, A-skips. Cue tall posture and controlled movement; ask how breathing and heart rate changed.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a dynamic warm-up?
questions.a: To raise heart rate and muscle temperature, increase range of motion, and prepare the nervous system for activity, lowering injury risk.

questions.q: Give a cue for an A-skip.
questions.a: Drive one knee up to hip height, stay tall on the ball of the opposite foot, and swing the opposite arm.

days.guide: After a 20-minute easy jog, model a 5–8 minute cool-down walk then static stretches held 15–30 seconds each for calves, hamstrings, quadriceps, hip flexors, chest, and shoulders. Check that the student breathes and does not bounce.

questions.q: How long should a static stretch be held?
questions.a: About 15–30 seconds (up to 60 for older adults), to mild tension, not pain.

questions.q: Why walk before stretching in a cool-down?
questions.a: To let heart rate and breathing return gradually toward resting and prevent blood pooling or dizziness.

days.guide: Teach heat exhaustion (heavy sweating, cool clammy skin, dizziness, nausea, headache — move to shade, cool, sip fluids) vs. heat stroke (body temperature 104°F+, confusion, possibly hot dry skin — call 911 and cool immediately). Then do a fartlek run in shade: easy jogging with unplanned surges to the next tree or post.

questions.q: A runner is confused and has hot skin after a run on a hot day. What do you do?
questions.a: Treat as possible heat stroke: call 911, move them to shade, and cool them rapidly (cold water, ice packs at neck/armpits/groin).

questions.q: What does 'fartlek' mean?
questions.a: Swedish for 'speed play' — continuous running with unstructured bursts of faster pace mixed with easy running.

days.guide: The student writes a warm-up (5–10 min, dynamic, specific to their workout) and a cool-down (walk plus 5–6 static stretches) and leads a family member through both. Watch for clear cues and safe demonstration.

questions.q: What should a warm-up include before a sprint workout specifically?
questions.a: General movement (easy jog), dynamic stretches for the legs and hips, then sport-specific drills and a few build-up strides (specificity).

days.guide: Have the student perform both routines while you check form, then give a short safety quiz (sample below).

questions.q: List three ways to prevent heat illness.
questions.a: Hydrate before/during/after, exercise in cooler times of day or shade, wear light breathable clothing, acclimatize gradually, and rest when symptoms start.

weeks.assessment_key: Routine demonstration: proficient = warm-up is dynamic and progressive, cool-down includes a gradual walk and static stretches held 15–30 s for major groups, cues are clear and form safe. Safety quiz key: 1) Heat exhaustion signs: heavy sweating, cool clammy skin, dizziness, nausea, headache, weakness. 2) Heat stroke signs: body temp ≥104°F, confusion/altered behavior, hot skin (may be dry), possible collapse. 3) Heat stroke first step: call 911 and cool rapidly. 4) Dynamic stretching before, static after. 5) Drink water before, during, and after activity; don't wait for thirst.

weeks.prep: Have a stopwatch or heart-rate app and a jump rope. Prepare a worked Karvonen example using the student's own age and resting heart rate from week 1. Have graph paper or a spreadsheet ready for Day 4.
misconceptions: Using 220 − age as an exact number. It is only an estimate (±10–12 bpm); RPE and the talk test help cross-check.
In the Karvonen formula, multiplying the percentage by maximum HR instead of heart rate reserve. Correct: THR = (HRmax − HRrest) × % + HRrest.
Counting the first beat as 'one' when starting a 15-second count. Start counting at zero on the first beat (or just be consistent) and multiply by 4.

days.guide: Walk through Karvonen: HRmax = 220 − age; HRR = HRmax − resting HR; THR = HRR × intensity% + resting HR. Work the example with the student's numbers, then they compute 50%, 60%, 70%, 85%. Check arithmetic.

questions.q: A 16-year-old has resting HR 70. Find her 60% and 70% target heart rates using Karvonen.
Using 220 − age only, what is 70% of max for a 17-year-old?

days.guide: Take pulse for 15 seconds × 4 at rest, after 3 min walking, after 3 min jogging, and after a 30-second sprint. The student records each with an RPE (1–10). Discuss how HR and RPE track together.

questions.q: You count 38 beats in 15 seconds. What is your heart rate?
What is the talk test?
questions.a: At moderate intensity you can talk but not sing; at vigorous intensity you can say only a few words before pausing for breath.

days.guide: Student runs 25 minutes aiming to stay in the 60–70% zone calculated Monday; stop briefly every 5 minutes for a 15-second pulse check and adjust pace. Record the five readings.

questions.q: Your check shows HR above your 70% zone. What do you do?
questions.a: Slow the pace (or walk briefly) until HR drops back into the 60–70% zone.

days.guide: Do 10 rounds of jump rope 30 s on/30 s off. Take pulse at the end of a work bout and again 1 minute after finishing; graph HR vs. time. Explain heart rate recovery: a faster drop indicates better aerobic fitness.

questions.q: HR is 180 at the end of exercise and 140 one minute later. What is the 1-minute recovery?
questions.a: 40 bpm drop — a larger drop generally indicates better cardiovascular fitness.

days.guide: Give the quiz below and review the heart-rate graph for labeled axes, units, and a one-sentence interpretation.

questions.q: Why might RPE be useful when a heart-rate monitor isn't available?
questions.a: RPE correlates with heart rate and intensity, so a person can judge effort by feel (on a 0–10 scale, about 5–6 is moderate and 7–8 is vigorous).

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) HRmax = 220 − age. 2) Karvonen THR = (HRmax − HRrest) × % + HRrest. 3) Age 15, rest 65, 70%: HRmax 205, HRR 140, 0.7 × 140 + 65 = 163 bpm. 4) 24 beats in 10 s = 144 bpm (×6). 5) On a 0–10 RPE scale, moderate ≈ 5–6 (can talk but not sing) and vigorous ≈ 7–8 (only a few words). Heart-rate graph rubric: proficient = time on x-axis, bpm on y-axis, labeled, all 10 intervals and the recovery point plotted, with a correct written interpretation of recovery.

weeks.prep: Ensure the student has supportive running shoes; set up a free route-mapping app (e.g., a GPS running app) and a training log with columns for date, distance, time, pace, RPE. Arrange access to a bike, pool, or rower for cross-training day.
misconceptions: Running every run hard. Most base training should be easy, conversational pace; hard days need easy days around them.
Overstriding (landing far in front with a heel) to go faster. Encourage quicker, shorter steps landing under the hips.
Thinking cross-training 'doesn't count.' Cycling or swimming builds the aerobic base while reducing impact stress.

days.guide: Teach run form: tall posture with slight forward lean from ankles, relaxed shoulders, arms swinging forward-back at ~90°, feet landing under the hips. Do drills (A-skips, butt kicks, strides). Count steps for 30 seconds and double to estimate cadence (aim ~160–180).

questions.q: You count 82 steps in 30 seconds. What is your cadence?
questions.a: 164 steps per minute.

questions.q: Name two cues for efficient running form.
questions.a: Run tall with a slight forward lean; land under the hips with quick light steps; relaxed shoulders; arms swing forward and back, not across the body.

days.guide: Student completes 30 minutes at conversational pace (talk test). Record distance, time, and compute average pace.

questions.q: You cover 3 miles in 33 minutes. What is your pace?
Why is 'long slow distance' useful?
questions.a: It builds the aerobic base — more capillaries and mitochondria and a stronger heart — with low injury and fatigue risk.

days.guide: Do 30 minutes of cycling, swimming, or rowing at moderate intensity (RPE 5–6). Discuss how it trains the same heart and lungs with different muscles and less impact.

questions.q: How does cross-training help a runner?
questions.a: It maintains or builds aerobic fitness while reducing repetitive impact stress, lowering overuse injury risk and adding variety.

days.guide: Explain tempo pace: 'comfortably hard' — RPE about 7, can say only a few words. Workout: 5 min easy, 10 min tempo, 5 min easy. Check HR at the end of the tempo portion.

questions.q: How should a tempo pace feel?
questions.a: Comfortably hard: sustained effort around RPE 7, breathing deep and rhythmic, only short phrases possible.

days.guide: Student completes 35 minutes easy and updates the log with weekly totals. Review the log together for completeness and an easy/hard pattern.

questions.q: What does the training log help you see?
questions.a: Weekly volume, pace trends, intensity (RPE), and whether you're progressing gradually or overdoing it.

weeks.assessment_key: Training log review rubric. 4 – All 5 sessions logged with date, type, time, distance, pace and RPE; weekly total calculated; a reflection notes trends and next-week adjustment. 3 (proficient) – All sessions logged with time, distance/type and RPE; total correct. 2 – Missing sessions or data columns. 1 – Log largely incomplete.

weeks.prep: Download an interval timer app; set cones 20 m apart for shuttles; find a moderate hill (30–60 seconds to climb). Review the student's target zones from week 4.
misconceptions: Believing HIIT should be done every day. It is stressful; 2–3 sessions per week with recovery days is plenty.
Thinking anaerobic means 'no oxygen in the body.' It means energy is produced without enough oxygen keeping up, so it can only be sustained briefly.
Using too little rest so quality drops. Work-to-rest ratios (e.g., 1:1 to 1:3) keep the work intervals truly hard.

days.guide: Explain energy systems: aerobic (with oxygen, long duration, lower intensity) vs. anaerobic (short, very intense bursts; produces fatigue quickly). Do a Tabata of squat jumps: 20 s work/10 s rest × 8 = 4 minutes.

questions.q: What is the structure of a Tabata?
questions.a: 8 rounds of 20 seconds all-out work and 10 seconds rest, totaling 4 minutes.

questions.q: Which energy system powers a 30-minute easy jog vs. a 20-second sprint?
questions.a: The jog is mostly aerobic; the 20-second sprint relies mostly on anaerobic systems (phosphocreatine and anaerobic glycolysis).

days.guide: Set cones 20 m apart. Student does 6 × 30-second shuttle runs (touch line, turn) with 90 seconds walking recovery. Count lengths each round to check if pace holds.

questions.q: What is the work-to-rest ratio of 30 s on/90 s off?

days.guide: Six hill repeats: drive knees, pump arms, lean slightly into the hill, short quick steps; walk or jog down for recovery. Watch for upright posture.

questions.q: Why are hill repeats useful?
questions.a: They build leg strength and power and raise intensity with less pounding than flat sprints.

days.guide: Student designs a 20-minute HIIT (warm-up, 4–6 exercises, work/rest ratio, cool-down) and completes it. Check that rest is adequate and exercises are safe.

questions.q: A HIIT plan has 45 s work and 15 s rest for 20 minutes of burpees. What would you change?
questions.a: Rest is too short for all-out work and a single exercise risks form breakdown; use 1:1 or 1:2 ratios, vary exercises, and include warm-up and cool-down.

days.guide: The student leads a family member through the workout, cueing form, then writes a comparison of HIIT vs. steady-state (time, intensity, benefits, risks).

questions.q: Give one advantage of HIIT and one of steady-state training.
questions.a: HIIT: improves fitness in less time and builds anaerobic capacity. Steady-state: lower injury/fatigue risk, builds aerobic base, easier to sustain and recover from.

weeks.assessment_key: HIIT design rubric. 4 – Includes warm-up, 4+ safe exercises, explicit work:rest ratio appropriate to intensity, cool-down, modifications, and correct HIIT vs. steady-state comparison. 3 (proficient) – Warm-up, exercises, safe ratio, cool-down, accurate comparison. 2 – Missing warm-up/cool-down or unsafe ratios. 1 – Incomplete plan.

weeks.prep: Measure a 5K (3.1-mile) route or register for a local fun run. Gather the student's training log and week 1 mile time. Have foam roller (optional) for recovery day.
misconceptions: Starting the race too fast. Even or negative splits (second half faster) usually produce better times.
Training hard the day before a race. Taper: reduce volume, keep a little intensity (strides).
Skipping recovery after a race. Gentle activity aids recovery more than total rest.

days.guide: Use the student's recent paces to set a goal 5K pace. Divide the 3.1 miles into splits and plan a strategy (start controlled, settle, push the last mile).

questions.q: A runner's goal 5K time is 27:54. What pace per mile is that?
What is a negative split?
questions.a: Running the second half of a race faster than the first half.

days.guide: 20-minute easy shake-out run plus 4–6 strides (20-second relaxed accelerations). Keep it easy.

questions.q: Why do a shake-out run before a race instead of a hard workout?
questions.a: To stay loose and keep legs fresh (taper) while not adding fatigue.

days.guide: Timed 5K (run, walk, or bike). Record total time and mile splits if possible; check that the student hydrates and warms up first.

questions.q: How many kilometers and miles is a 5K?
questions.a: 5 kilometers ≈ 3.1 miles.

days.guide: Easy walk 20–30 min, foam rolling of calves/quads, and static stretching. Discuss soreness vs. pain.

questions.q: How can you tell normal muscle soreness from injury?
questions.a: Soreness is dull, in both legs or muscles broadly, and improves within 1–3 days; injury pain is sharp, localized, worsens with activity, or causes limping — stop and seek care.

days.guide: Student compares 5K average pace to week 1 mile pace and writes a reflection; update SMART goals if needed.

questions.q: Why might 5K pace per mile be slower than a single mile's pace?
questions.a: Longer distances must be run at a lower intensity to be sustained, so pace per mile is usually slower.

weeks.assessment_key: 5K reflection rubric. 4 – Records time and splits, calculates average pace correctly, compares to week 1 mile pace with explanation, evaluates pacing strategy and sets a revised goal. 3 (proficient) – Time, correct pace, comparison, and updated goal. 2 – Time recorded but comparison/goal missing. 1 – Incomplete. (No time standard is required; effort and accurate reflection are graded.)

weeks.prep: Gather an exercise mat and resistance bands; set up a phone to record form video. Find a sturdy table for inverted rows (test that it won't tip) or use a band row instead. Preview a muscle diagram.
misconceptions: Believing lifting makes teens 'bulky' or stunts growth. Supervised, technique-focused resistance training is safe and beneficial for teens.
Letting knees cave in during squats. Cue 'knees track over toes' and push the floor apart.
Sagging hips in push-ups. The body should be a straight plank from head to heels; regress to incline push-ups if form breaks.

days.guide: Show a muscle diagram and name major groups: chest (pectorals), back (latissimus dorsi, trapezius), shoulders (deltoids), arms (biceps, triceps), core (abdominals, obliques), legs (quadriceps, hamstrings, glutes, calves). Explain adaptation: neural gains first, then hypertrophy. Do a bodyweight circuit (squats, push-ups, glute bridges, plank) ×3.

questions.q: In a biceps curl, what are the concentric and eccentric phases?
questions.a: Concentric: lifting the weight as the biceps shortens. Eccentric: lowering it as the biceps lengthens under control.

questions.q: Why do beginners gain strength quickly in the first few weeks?
questions.a: Mostly neural adaptations — better recruitment and coordination of muscle fibers — before significant muscle growth.

days.guide: Teach the bodyweight squat (feet shoulder-width, hips back and down, chest up, knees over toes, depth to at least parallel if comfortable), then goblet squat holding a jug at the chest. Record a side and front video and review.

questions.q: Name three squat form cues.
questions.a: Chest up, sit hips back and down, knees track over toes, weight across the whole foot, neutral spine.

days.guide: Progress push-ups from wall → incline (counter) → full; student finds the level they can do 8–12 good reps. Then band chest press (band behind back). Check straight body line.

questions.q: What muscles does a push-up mainly work?
questions.a: Pectorals (chest), anterior deltoids (front shoulders), triceps, with the core stabilizing.

days.guide: Teach band rows (squeeze shoulder blades, elbows close) and inverted rows under a sturdy table (body straight, pull chest to table). Test table safety first.

questions.q: What muscles do rows mainly work?
questions.a: Back muscles — latissimus dorsi, rhomboids, middle trapezius — plus biceps and rear deltoids.

days.guide: Use a form checklist to score squat, push, and pull (3 reps each). Give specific feedback and a regression/progression for each.

questions.q: Define a set and a repetition.
questions.a: A repetition is one complete movement; a set is a group of consecutive repetitions (e.g., 3 sets of 10 reps).

weeks.assessment_key: Form checklist (1 point each, proficient ≥ 8/10). Squat: chest up; hips back; knees track toes; heels down; depth to parallel or comfortable. Push-up: straight body line; elbows ~45° from body; chest to fist height/full range. Row: shoulder blades squeeze; torso stable/no swinging.

weeks.prep: Gather light dumbbells or filled water jugs (a gallon of water ≈ 8.3 lb), resistance bands, a dowel or broomstick, and a sturdy step or stair. Set up video recording.
misconceptions: Rounding the back in a hinge. The dowel should touch head, upper back, and tailbone throughout.
Squatting a deadlift. A hinge moves mainly at the hips with a slight knee bend; a squat bends knees and hips more equally.
Letting the front knee collapse inward in lunges or step-ups. Keep the knee in line with the second toe.

days.guide: Hold a dowel along the spine (three points of contact). Push hips back with soft knees until hamstrings stretch, then drive hips forward. Progress to Romanian deadlifts with light jugs, 3×10.

questions.q: What muscles does the Romanian deadlift target?
questions.a: Hamstrings and glutes, with spinal erectors stabilizing.

questions.q: How does the dowel help in learning the hinge?
questions.a: If it loses contact with the head, upper back, or tailbone, the spine is rounding or arching — it gives feedback for a neutral spine.

days.guide: Teach forward, reverse, and lateral lunges: long enough stride, torso tall, back knee toward floor, front knee over ankle. 2×8 each leg each variation.

questions.q: Which lunge is usually easier on the knees for beginners, forward or reverse?
questions.a: Reverse lunge — the front shin stays more vertical and braking forces are lower.

days.guide: Step-ups onto a sturdy step (whole foot on step, drive through heel, control the descent), 3×10 each leg; calf raises 3×15 with a pause at the top.

questions.q: Which muscles do calf raises strengthen?
questions.a: Gastrocnemius and soleus (calves).

days.guide: Full lower-body workout: goblet squat, RDL, reverse lunge, step-up, calf raise — 3 sets of 10–12, rest 60–90 s. Log loads and RPE.

questions.q: Why rest 60–90 seconds between sets?
questions.a: To partially recover so the next set can be done with good form and similar effort, appropriate for muscular endurance/hypertrophy work.

days.guide: Student records a set of each exercise and self-assesses with the checklist; log the workout.

questions.q: In your video, how would you know if your hinge is correct?
questions.a: Back stays flat, hips move back (not down), shins nearly vertical, feel stretch in hamstrings.

weeks.assessment_key: Video form check (proficient = correct on at least 4 of 5 exercises). RDL: neutral spine, hips back, slight knee bend. Squat: chest up, knees track toes, depth. Lunge: torso tall, front knee over ankle, controlled descent. Step-up: whole foot on step, drive through heel, controlled lowering. Calf raise: full range, pause at top. Self-assessment must name one strength and one correction.

weeks.prep: Gather dumbbells or jugs, resistance bands (anchor point such as a door anchor), and a mat. Preview the dead bug and bird dog movements so you can demonstrate.
misconceptions: Arching the lower back when pressing overhead. Brace the core and squeeze glutes; reduce the load if needed.
Thinking 'core' means just sit-ups. Core training emphasizes stability — resisting movement (anti-extension, anti-rotation).
Holding the breath for long sets. Exhale on the effort phase; brief bracing is fine.

days.guide: Teach overhead press (feet hip-width, brace core, press straight up, biceps by ears) and lateral raises (slight elbow bend, raise to shoulder height). 3×10 each with light load.

questions.q: Which muscle does a lateral raise mainly target?
questions.a: The deltoids (especially the middle/lateral deltoid).

days.guide: Teach plank, side plank, dead bug, and bird dog. Cue neutral spine and slow movement. Hold or do 3 rounds.

questions.q: What is the main job of the core in a plank?
questions.a: Anti-extension — preventing the lower back from sagging, keeping a neutral spine.

questions.q: In a dead bug, what should the low back do?
questions.a: Stay gently pressed toward the floor while opposite arm and leg extend.

days.guide: Anchor a band at chest height; stand sideways, press hands straight out and resist the band's pull to rotate. 3×10 each side.

questions.q: Why is the Pallof press called 'anti-rotation'?
questions.a: The band pulls the body to rotate, and the core works to resist that rotation and keep the torso square.

days.guide: Upper body and core workout: overhead press, band row or inverted row, push-up, lateral raise, plank, Pallof press. 3 sets; log.

questions.q: Name the large back muscle worked in rows and pulldowns.
questions.a: The latissimus dorsi ('lats').

days.guide: Review the week's log; student writes what improved and one goal for next week.

questions.q: If all your sets of 10 felt easy (RPE 5), what should you do next week?
questions.a: Apply progressive overload — add load or reps (e.g., 12 reps or a slightly heavier weight).

weeks.assessment_key: Workout log rubric. 4 – All sessions logged with exercises, sets, reps, loads, RPE, and a reflection that names progress and a specific progression for next week. 3 (proficient) – Complete exercise/set/rep/load data and a short reflection. 2 – Partial log. 1 – Minimal data.

weeks.prep: Print a 4-week program template (exercise, sets, reps, load, rest, weekly progression). Gather dumbbells/jugs/bands. Review RPE and reps in reserve (RIR).
misconceptions: Choosing a split routine with too few days to hit each muscle group. With 3 days/week, full-body sessions are usually best for beginners.
Picking loads that are far too easy or to failure every set. Aim for 2–3 reps in reserve.
Changing exercises every session. Consistency is needed to measure progression.

days.guide: Compare full-body (all major groups each session, 2–3 days/week) vs. split (e.g., upper/lower on different days, 4+ days). Student picks one and explains why. Do a 25-minute bodyweight circuit.

questions.q: Why is a full-body routine good for someone training 3 days a week?
questions.a: Each muscle group is trained 3 times weekly with rest days between, giving good frequency and recovery.

days.guide: Teach RIR: after a set, how many more good reps could you have done? Test goblet squat, row, and press loads to find a weight leaving 2–3 RIR at 10 reps.

questions.q: You do 10 reps and could have done 2 more. What is your RIR and approximate RPE?
questions.a: RIR 2 ≈ RPE 8.

days.guide: Student writes a 4-week, 3-day full-body program: Workout A (squat, push, hinge, core) and B (lunge, pull, press, carry), alternating, with sets × reps, rest, and a progression rule (e.g., add 1–2 reps per week then increase load).

questions.q: Give a simple progression rule for a 4-week program.
questions.a: Example (double progression): stay at the same load and add reps from 8 to 12; when all sets reach 12, increase the load and drop back to 8.

days.guide: Complete Workout A and log loads and RPE.

questions.q: Why log RPE in addition to load?
questions.a: RPE shows how hard the load felt, helping decide when to progress or back off.

days.guide: Complete Workout B (including a farmer's carry with jugs) and submit the program.

questions.q: What does a farmer's carry train?
questions.a: Grip strength, core stability, posture, and overall work capacity.

weeks.assessment_key: Strength program rubric. 4 – 4 weeks, 3 days/week, alternates A/B covering squat, hinge, push, pull, lunge, press, core, carry; specifies sets, reps, rest, starting loads (2–3 RIR), clear weekly progression, warm-up and cool-down, safety notes. 3 (proficient) – All movement patterns, sets/reps/rest, and a progression. 2 – Missing patterns or progression. 1 – Incomplete.

weeks.prep: Gather the fitness journal with week 1 push-up and curl-up results and the strength logs; graph paper or a spreadsheet. Prepare the unit quiz (key below).
misconceptions: Expecting linear progress forever. Plateaus are normal; change variables (reps, rest, exercise) or deload.
Testing on a tired day. Retests should follow a rest day and the same protocol as baseline.
Attributing all change to one factor. Consider training, sleep, nutrition, and technique.

days.guide: Repeat Workout A adding one rep or a small load increase per exercise; log.

questions.q: What is progressive overload?
questions.a: Gradually increasing training demands (load, reps, sets, or difficulty) so the body keeps adapting.

days.guide: Retest 90° push-ups and curl-ups with cadence, plus a max plank hold with good form. Compare to week 1.

questions.q: Why must the retest use the same protocol as baseline?
questions.a: So the comparison is valid — changes reflect fitness, not different test conditions.

days.guide: Repeat Workout B with progression; log.

questions.q: What is a plateau, and one way to break it?
questions.a: A period with no improvement; change a variable (rep range, exercise, volume), deload for a week, or improve sleep/nutrition.

days.guide: Student graphs baseline vs. retest (bar graph) and writes an explanation of changes.

questions.q: Push-ups went from 12 to 18. What is the percent increase?

days.guide: Give the unit quiz.

questions.q: Name one muscle group for each: squat, row, overhead press.
questions.a: Squat: quadriceps/glutes; row: latissimus dorsi/rhomboids; press: deltoids/triceps.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit quiz key: 1) Concentric = muscle shortens under load; eccentric = lengthens under control. 2) Progressive overload = gradually increasing demand. 3) Specificity = adaptations match the training. 4) Squat works quads, glutes, hamstrings. 5) Rows work lats, rhomboids, biceps. 6) Safety: warm up, use correct form, appropriate load, controlled tempo, clear space, never hold breath for long. 7) RIR 2 = could do 2 more reps. 8) Beginners' early gains are mostly neural. Retest rubric: proficient = all retests done with correct protocol, graphed against baseline, and changes explained with reasons.

weeks.prep: Gather a mat, towel or strap, optional foam roller, and the sit-and-reach box. Read about PNF contract-relax so you can partner safely (gentle pressure only).
misconceptions: Thinking flexibility is fixed. Regular stretching improves range of motion within weeks.
Stretching into pain. Stretch to mild tension; pain signals risk of injury.
Pushing hard as the partner in PNF. The partner only holds the position; the stretcher controls intensity.

days.guide: Explain static (hold), dynamic (controlled movement through range), and PNF (contract then relax to stretch further). Retest sit-and-reach and compare to week 1.

questions.q: Which type of stretching is best before a sprint workout, and which after?
questions.a: Dynamic before; static (and PNF) after or in separate flexibility sessions.

days.guide: Lead a 20-minute hip and hamstring routine: 90/90 hip switches, pigeon stretch, supine strap hamstring stretch, hip flexor lunge. Hold 30 s; breathe.

questions.q: Why might tight hip flexors matter for people who sit a lot?
questions.a: Prolonged sitting keeps the hip flexors shortened, which can limit hip extension and contribute to poor posture or low-back discomfort.

days.guide: Thoracic rotations (open books), wall slides, and cat-cow. Assess shoulder flexibility with the Fitnessgram shoulder stretch (reach one hand over the shoulder and the other up the back; do fingers touch?).

questions.q: How is the Fitnessgram shoulder stretch scored?
questions.a: Pass ('Y') if fingertips touch behind the back on that side; tested on both sides.

days.guide: Contract-relax: partner holds the student's straight leg at a mild stretch; student pushes the leg against the partner at ~25–50% effort for 6 seconds, relaxes, then gently moves further into the stretch for 20–30 s. Repeat 3 times each leg.

questions.q: Describe contract-relax PNF in order.
questions.a: Stretch to mild tension, isometrically contract the muscle against resistance ~6 s, relax, then move into a deeper stretch and hold.

questions.q: What is the partner's safety role?
questions.a: Hold the limb steady, apply only gentle pressure, and stop immediately if the stretcher says to.

days.guide: Student designs and performs a 15-minute routine targeting their tight areas, with hold times.

questions.q: Why is foam rolling used?
questions.a: It may reduce perceived tightness and soreness and temporarily improve range of motion.

weeks.assessment_key: Mobility routine rubric. 4 – 15 minutes, targets the student's measured tight areas (cites sit-and-reach/shoulder results), includes dynamic and static elements with correct hold times (15–30 s), safe technique cues, and a frequency plan. 3 (proficient) – Covers hips, hamstrings, shoulders, spine with correct hold times and safe form. 2 – Incomplete or incorrect hold times. 1 – Not performed.

weeks.prep: Gather a mat and choose a free beginner yoga video (e.g., Yoga with Adriene's beginner sessions); preview it. Prepare a stress rating (1–10) sheet for before/after.
misconceptions: Forcing poses to look like a photo. Use props and modifications; alignment and breathing matter more than depth.
Holding the breath in difficult poses. Breath should stay smooth; if it can't, ease out.
Locking (hyperextending) knees in standing poses. Keep a micro-bend.

days.guide: Teach diaphragmatic breathing (hand on belly rises on inhale) and box breathing (inhale 4, hold 4, exhale 4, hold 4). Practice 5 minutes; rate stress before and after in the journal.

questions.q: Describe box breathing.
questions.a: Inhale for 4 counts, hold 4, exhale 4, hold 4; repeat.

questions.q: How does slow breathing reduce stress?
questions.a: Slow exhalation activates the parasympathetic ('rest and digest') nervous system, lowering heart rate and arousal.

days.guide: Teach mountain, warrior I, warrior II, triangle, and tree with cues: front knee over ankle in warriors, hips square in warrior I and open in warrior II, foot on calf or thigh (never on the knee) in tree.

questions.q: Where should the lifted foot go in tree pose?
questions.a: On the inner calf or inner thigh — never pressing on the side of the knee.

questions.q: What is a key difference between warrior I and warrior II?
questions.a: Warrior I hips face forward with arms overhead; warrior II hips open to the side with arms extended parallel to the floor.

days.guide: Teach sun salutation A step by step (mountain, upward salute, forward fold, half lift, plank/chaturanga, upward dog or cobra, downward dog, step forward, fold, rise), linking breath; do five rounds.

questions.q: What does 'vinyasa' mean in yoga practice?
questions.a: Linking breath with movement in a flowing sequence.

days.guide: Follow a 40-minute guided practice. Afterwards discuss which poses were hardest and why.

questions.q: Name a benefit of regular yoga.
questions.a: Improved flexibility, balance, and strength, plus reduced stress and better breath control.

days.guide: Student performs a 10-pose sequence while you check alignment, then writes a stress reflection.

questions.q: What is an alignment cue for downward dog?
questions.a: Hands shoulder-width, push the floor away, hips lift up and back, long spine; heels reach toward the floor (bent knees are fine).

weeks.assessment_key: Pose sequence demonstration rubric. 4 – 10 poses flow smoothly with breath, correct alignment cues in each (e.g., knee over ankle, foot off knee in tree), modifications used appropriately, thoughtful reflection on stress change using before/after ratings. 3 (proficient) – 10 poses with mostly correct alignment and steady breath; reflection included. 2 – Several alignment errors or missing poses. 1 – Incomplete.

weeks.prep: Gather a mat and a firm pillow or cushion for balance work. Preview the Pilates hundred, roll-up, and single-leg stretch. Prepare the unit quiz and the flexibility log.
misconceptions: Doing the hundred with neck strain. Support the head or keep it down; the work comes from the abdominals.
Thinking balance only matters for athletes. Balance and proprioception prevent falls and ankle injuries at every age.
Believing more screen time before bed helps relaxation. Bright screens can delay sleep; build a screen-free wind-down.

days.guide: Teach neutral spine (natural curve, not flattened or arched). Teach the hundred (pump arms, inhale 5 counts, exhale 5, ×10), the roll-up, and single-leg stretch.

questions.q: What does 'neutral spine' mean?
questions.a: Keeping the spine's natural curves — not pressing the low back flat nor arching excessively.

questions.q: How many pumps in the Pilates hundred?
questions.a: 100 arm pumps: 10 breath cycles of 5 pumps inhaling and 5 exhaling.

days.guide: Progress single-leg balance: eyes open 30 s, eyes closed, on a pillow, eyes closed on a pillow. Record times for each leg.

questions.q: What is proprioception?
questions.a: The body's sense of its position and movement, from receptors in muscles, tendons, and joints.

questions.q: Why is balance harder with eyes closed?
questions.a: Vision is one of the main balance inputs; without it, you rely on proprioception and the inner ear.

days.guide: Complete a 30-minute session combining Pilates mat moves and balance drills.

questions.q: Name two muscles groups Pilates emphasizes.
questions.a: Deep abdominals (transverse abdominis) and the muscles of the back/hips that stabilize the trunk.

days.guide: Read about exercise, sleep, and cortisol. Student plans a nightly wind-down (consistent bedtime, no screens 30–60 min before, stretching/breathing, cool dark room).

questions.q: How does regular exercise affect stress hormones and sleep?
questions.a: Regular exercise helps regulate cortisol and stress responses and generally improves sleep quality — though intense exercise right before bed may delay sleep for some people.

days.guide: Give the quiz and update sit-and-reach in the flexibility log.

questions.q: Which stretching method uses a muscle contraction followed by a stretch?
questions.a: PNF (proprioceptive neuromuscular facilitation), e.g., contract-relax.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) Static = hold; dynamic = controlled movement; PNF = contract then stretch. 2) Hold static stretches 15–30 s. 3) Proprioception = body position sense. 4) Neutral spine = natural curves. 5) Diaphragmatic breathing = belly rises on inhale. 6) Teens need 8–10 hours of sleep. 7) Benefits of flexibility: range of motion, posture, possibly fewer injuries. Flexibility log: proficient = sit-and-reach (both sides) recorded weeks 1, 13, 15 with a sentence on change.

weeks.prep: Get paddles and a pickleball (perforated plastic) or locate a public court; find a smooth wall. Read the USA Pickleball basics: underhand serve, double-bounce rule, non-volley zone (kitchen, 7 ft from net), doubles scoring.
misconceptions: Volleying while standing in the kitchen. You may not volley (hit before the bounce) with any part of your body in the non-volley zone, including momentum carrying you in.
Thinking the receiving team can score. Only the serving side scores points.
Rushing the net immediately after serving. The double-bounce rule means the return must bounce, so the serving team usually stays back for the third shot.

days.guide: Teach continental grip ('shake hands' with the paddle). Forehand and backhand against a wall: short backswing, contact in front, follow through toward target. 50 each.

questions.q: Describe the continental grip.
questions.a: Hold the paddle like shaking hands, with the 'V' between thumb and index finger on top of the handle — it works for both forehand and backhand.

days.guide: Teach the serve: underhand, contact below the waist, upward arc, cross-court into the diagonal service box, beyond the kitchen line. Practice serves and deep returns. Explain double-bounce: serve must bounce, and the return must bounce before either team may volley.

questions.q: State the double-bounce rule.
questions.a: After the serve, the ball must bounce once on each side (the return of serve and the third shot) before players may volley.

questions.q: Where must a serve land?
questions.a: In the diagonal service court, past the non-volley zone line (a serve landing on the kitchen line is a fault).

days.guide: At the kitchen line, practice soft dinks that arc over the net and land in the opponent's kitchen. Explain kitchen rules.

questions.q: Can you step into the kitchen to hit a ball that bounced there?
questions.a: Yes — you may enter the kitchen anytime to play a ball that has bounced; you may not volley while in it.

days.guide: Teach doubles scoring: score called as serving team, receiving team, server number (game starts 0-0-2); games to 11, win by 2. Play practice games.

questions.q: Why does a doubles game start at '0-0-2'?
questions.a: The first serving team gets only one server before the first side-out, so play starts as if it were the second server.

questions.q: What score wins a standard game?
questions.a: 11 points, winning by at least 2.

days.guide: Skill check: 10 serves (target 7 in), 20-dink cooperative rally; give rules quiz.

questions.q: What is a 'third-shot drop'?
questions.a: A soft shot by the serving team on the third shot that lands in the opponent's kitchen, allowing the servers to move up to the net.

weeks.assessment_key: Skill check: proficient = 7/10 legal serves and a 20-dink rally. Rules quiz key: 1) Kitchen = non-volley zone, 7 ft from the net. 2) Serve underhand, contact below waist, cross-court, past the kitchen. 3) Double-bounce rule (each side lets ball bounce once). 4) Only serving team scores. 5) Games to 11, win by 2. 6) Score call = server score, receiver score, server number. 7) A ball landing on a line (except kitchen line on serve) is in.

weeks.prep: Get badminton rackets and shuttles, or book time at a community center gym. Mark six 'corners' with cones on a rough court (front, mid, back on each side). Read badminton rally scoring: to 21, win by 2, cap 30.
misconceptions: Hitting overhead shots with a stiff arm. Power comes from the kinetic chain: legs, hips, trunk rotation, then shoulder, elbow, wrist/forearm.
Staying where you hit. Return to base (center) after every shot.
Thinking only the server scores (that was the old system). Badminton uses rally scoring — a point on every rally.

days.guide: Teach the forehand grip and overhead clear: turn sideways, racket up, reach high, rotate and hit high and deep to the back. 30 clears.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a clear?
questions.a: To hit high and deep to the opponent's back court, buying time and pushing them back.

days.guide: Practice the drop (looks like a clear, softly lands near the net) and the smash (steep, powerful downward shot). Emphasize the same preparation for deception and the kinetic chain.

questions.q: Why use the same preparation for clear, drop, and smash?
questions.a: Deception — the opponent can't tell which shot is coming until late.

questions.q: Describe the kinetic chain in a smash.
questions.a: Force is transferred sequentially from the legs through hip and trunk rotation to the shoulder, elbow, forearm, and wrist.

days.guide: Teach base position (center, slight crouch, racket up) and six-corner footwork: move to each cone with chasse steps or a lunge and return to base. Repeat in sets of 30 s.

questions.q: Why return to base after each shot?
questions.a: It minimizes the distance to any next shot so you can cover the whole court.

days.guide: Play games with the strategy goal of moving the opponent front to back (clear then drop). Teach rally scoring to 21.

questions.q: Describe badminton singles scoring.
questions.a: Rally scoring: a point on every rally; games to 21, win by 2, capped at 30 (30-29 wins).

days.guide: Skill test: 10 clears to the back third and 10 drops to the front third; student writes a pickleball vs. badminton strategy comparison.

questions.q: How is strategy similar in pickleball and badminton?
questions.a: Both use placement and changes of depth/pace to move opponents and create openings; both reward patience and returning to a ready position.

weeks.assessment_key: Skill test: proficient = 6/10 clears land in back third and 6/10 drops land in front third with correct grip and preparation. Comparison rubric: proficient answer notes similarities (placement, moving opponents, ready position) and differences (pickleball's kitchen and double-bounce rule and soft game vs. badminton's overhead power shots, shuttle never bounces, rally scoring to 21 vs. pickleball's side-out scoring to 11).

weeks.prep: Gather stopwatch, measuring tape, sit-and-reach box, the journal with week 1 data and HFZ charts. Use the same mile route as week 1.
misconceptions: Comparing to others instead of to your own baseline. Focus on personal change and HFZ.
Assuming no improvement means training failed. Consider test-day factors (sleep, weather) and look at multiple measures.
Writing goals that are already met. Revise goals upward or toward new components.

days.guide: Take resting HR on waking or after 5 minutes seated. Warm up and run the mile; record time.

questions.q: Resting HR dropped from 78 to 70. What might that indicate?
questions.a: Improved cardiovascular fitness — a stronger heart pumps more blood per beat, so it needs fewer beats at rest.

days.guide: Retest push-ups and curl-ups with cadence, and trunk lift.

questions.q: Why use the same cadence as the baseline?
questions.a: So results are comparable and form standards are identical.

days.guide: Retest sit-and-reach (both sides) and the shoulder stretch.

questions.q: Which muscles does the sit-and-reach mainly measure?
questions.a: Hamstrings (and to some degree the lower back).

days.guide: Student builds a table and bar graph: baseline vs. midyear for each test, with HFZ lines.

questions.q: Mile time improved from 10:40 to 9:52. How many seconds faster?
questions.a: 48 seconds faster (640 s − 592 s).

days.guide: Student writes a semester reflection and revises SMART goals.

questions.q: Name one revised goal type for spring.
questions.a: Example: maintain HFZ in aerobic capacity while raising push-ups from 18 to 25 by May 15.

weeks.assessment_key: Semester fitness report rubric. 4 – All tests retested with correct protocol, a labeled comparison table/graph with HFZ, correct calculations of change, analysis linking results to training, and revised SMART goals. 3 (proficient) – Complete data, graph, explanation, revised goals. 2 – Partial data or analysis. 1 – Incomplete.

weeks.prep: Locate a public tennis court and wall; gather a racket and balls. Read tennis scoring (love, 15, 30, 40, deuce, advantage) and basic etiquette. Choose a racquet sport for the Day 4 round-robin and invite players.
misconceptions: Swinging only with the arm. Turn the shoulders and step into the ball.
Calling the score with the receiver's score first. The server's score is announced first.
Thinking a let serve is a fault. A serve that clips the net and lands in the correct box is replayed (let).

days.guide: Teach the forehand (turn, racket back, low-to-high swing, contact in front, follow through over the shoulder) and two-handed backhand. Rally against a wall.

questions.q: How does a low-to-high swing create topspin?
questions.a: Brushing up the back of the ball makes it spin forward, so it dips down into the court and bounces high.

days.guide: Teach the flat serve: toss slightly in front, 'trophy position' (racket back, tossing arm up), reach up and swing through. Serve into the diagonal service box.

questions.q: Into which box must the first serve of a game go?
questions.a: The diagonally opposite service box — from the right (deuce) side into the opponent's right service box crosswise.

questions.q: What is the trophy position?
questions.a: Mid-serve position with the tossing arm pointing up, racket arm bent behind the head, knees bent — resembling a trophy figure.

days.guide: Teach scoring: 0 (love), 15, 30, 40, game; 40-40 is deuce; next point is advantage; win by two points. Games to 6 win by 2 for a set. Etiquette: call your own lines fairly, wait for points to finish before crossing courts, return stray balls.

questions.q: The score is 40-30 and the receiver wins the next point. What is the score?
What is a 'let' on a serve?
questions.a: The serve touches the net and lands in the correct box; it is replayed with no penalty.

days.guide: Hold a round-robin with family/friends in the chosen racquet sport. Student keeps a results table and practices sportsmanship and self-officiating.

questions.q: In a 4-player round-robin, how many matches are played?
questions.a: 6 (each player plays the other 3; 4×3÷2 = 6).

days.guide: Student completes self and peer evaluations on skill and sportsmanship.

questions.q: Give one example of good sportsmanship in racquet sports.
questions.a: Making honest line calls, shaking hands or tapping paddles after play, and complimenting opponents' good shots.

weeks.assessment_key: Tournament evaluation rubric (skills and sportsmanship). 4 – Consistent legal serves, controlled rallies, correct scoring called aloud, fair line calls, encourages others, accurate self/peer reflection. 3 (proficient) – Mostly consistent strokes, correct scoring, good etiquette, completed reflection. 2 – Frequent errors or scoring confusion; some etiquette lapses. 1 – Unsafe or unsportsmanlike behavior.

weeks.prep: Gather a daypack, water, layers, sunscreen, first-aid kit, headlamp, map/app. Check California State Parks or trail apps for a 3–5 mile trail; check weather, closures, and fire conditions. Tell someone the plan. Parent should accompany the hike.
misconceptions: Relying only on a phone for navigation. Batteries die and signal fails; carry a paper map and know the route.
Underestimating time on hills. Add time for elevation gain (Naismith-style rule: roughly 1 extra hour per 2,000 ft of gain, on top of ~2 mph walking).
Thinking biodegradable trash (orange peels) is fine to leave. Leave No Trace: pack it in, pack it out.

days.guide: List the Ten Essentials and pack a daypack together. Discuss why each is needed.

questions.q: Name the Ten Essentials.
questions.a: Navigation (map/compass/GPS), headlamp, sun protection, first aid, knife/repair kit, fire (matches/lighter), emergency shelter, extra food, extra water, extra clothes.

days.guide: Student uses a trail app or State Parks site to choose a 3–5 mile route; record distance, elevation gain, and estimate time (~2 mph + 1 hour per 2,000 ft gain). Include a turnaround time.

questions.q: Estimate hiking time for 4 miles with 1,000 ft gain.
questions.a: About 2 hours for distance (4 ÷ 2 mph) + 0.5 hour for gain = about 2.5 hours, plus breaks.

days.guide: 45-minute walk with a pack weighted with water bottles, on hills or stairs.

questions.q: Why train with a loaded pack?
questions.a: Specificity — it prepares the legs, back, and feet for carrying weight on hills.

days.guide: Do the hike. Practice the 7 Leave No Trace principles and trail etiquette (uphill hikers have right of way; yield to horses; stay on trail).

questions.q: Who has the right-of-way on a trail: uphill or downhill hikers?
questions.a: Uphill hikers generally have the right-of-way; downhill hikers step aside.

questions.q: Name three Leave No Trace principles.
questions.a: Plan ahead and prepare; travel and camp on durable surfaces; dispose of waste properly; leave what you find; minimize campfire impacts; respect wildlife; be considerate of other visitors.

days.guide: Student submits a trip report: route, distance, elevation, time, HR data, conditions, and reflections.

questions.q: What is elevation gain?
questions.a: The total vertical distance climbed during the hike.

weeks.assessment_key: Trip report rubric. 4 – Route map, distance, elevation gain, total time, HR data with interpretation, Ten Essentials checklist, Leave No Trace practices described, reflection. 3 (proficient) – Route, distance, elevation, time, HR, reflection. 2 – Missing key data. 1 – Minimal.

weeks.prep: Get a baseplate compass and print a park map (topographic if possible). Measure a 100 m course (e.g., a track straightaway is ~100 m). Prepare 8 flags or markers and design a simple course with bearings and distances. Note that in California magnetic declination is roughly 11–13° east.
misconceptions: Holding the compass near metal or a phone, which deflects the needle.
Reading contour lines as trails. Contour lines connect points of equal elevation; close together = steep.
Following the needle instead of the direction-of-travel arrow. 'Red in the shed': align the north needle with the orienting arrow, then walk where the direction-of-travel arrow points.

days.guide: Teach map legend, scale, and contour lines. Have the student find the steepest slope and a hilltop on a topo map.

questions.q: What does it mean when contour lines are close together?
questions.a: The terrain is steep.

questions.q: A map scale is 1:24,000. How far is 1 inch on the map?
questions.a: 24,000 inches = 2,000 feet on the ground.

days.guide: Teach compass parts; take a bearing to an object (point direction-of-travel arrow, rotate housing until orienting arrow aligns with the red needle, read the degrees). Then follow a given bearing.

questions.q: What bearing is due east? Due south-west?
questions.a: East = 90°; southwest = 225°.

questions.q: What is the back bearing of 70°?

days.guide: Walk 100 m counting every time the same foot lands (double paces). Repeat 3 times and average. Practice estimating a 50 m distance.

questions.q: Your pace count is 64 per 100 m. How many paces for 250 m?

days.guide: Family sets 8 control points; student navigates using bearings and pace counts, recording control codes. Time the course.

questions.q: What is a control point in orienteering?
questions.a: A marked checkpoint on the course that the navigator must find and record in order.

days.guide: Navigation test: take/follow bearings, read map features, compute distances with scale and pace count.

questions.q: Why adjust for declination?
questions.a: Magnetic north differs from true (map) north; in California the compass needle points about 11–13° east of true north, so bearings must be corrected.

weeks.assessment_key: Navigation test key (sample): 1) North 0°/360°, east 90°, south 180°, west 270°. 2) Back bearing of 120° = 300°. 3) Close contour lines = steep slope; concentric rings = hilltop. 4) On a 1:24,000 map, 3 inches = 6,000 ft. 5) Pace count 60/100 m → 300 m = 180 paces. 6) Practical: follow a 3-leg course to within ~10 m of each target. Proficient = 80%+ written and all practical legs completed.

weeks.prep: Check the bicycle (tires, brakes, chain) and helmet fit. Identify a low-traffic area or bike path for skills practice. Look up local bike lanes and a route to a frequent destination. Parent should ride along or supervise traffic practice.
misconceptions: Riding against traffic. Cyclists ride in the same direction as traffic, as far right as practicable (California Vehicle Code).
Wearing a helmet tilted back. It should sit level, about two finger-widths above the eyebrows.
Assuming drivers see you. Make eye contact, use lights, and signal clearly.

days.guide: ABC quick check: Air (squeeze tires/check PSI on sidewall), Brakes (squeeze, wheels lock), Chain/cranks (clean, spins smoothly); also quick releases. Helmet fit: level, 2 fingers above eyebrows, straps form a V under each ear, 1–2 fingers under chin strap.

questions.q: What does ABC stand for in the quick check?
questions.a: Air, Brakes, Chain (cranks), followed by Quick releases and a Check ride.

questions.q: Describe correct helmet fit.
questions.a: Level on the head, about two finger-widths above the eyebrows, side straps form a V just below each ear, chin strap snug with room for about one finger.

days.guide: In a safe area, practice hand signals, looking over the shoulder without swerving, and straight-line riding as if in a bike lane.

questions.q: Show the hand signals for left turn, right turn, and stop.
questions.a: Left: left arm straight out. Right: left arm bent up at 90° (or right arm straight out). Stop/slow: left arm bent down.

days.guide: Ride 45–60 minutes at moderate intensity (RPE 5–6); record distance and HR.

questions.q: What cadence (pedal rpm) is efficient for most riders?
questions.a: About 70–90 rpm; use gears to keep cadence steady.

days.guide: Map a route to a common destination using bike lanes/quiet streets; ride or walk it with a parent.

questions.q: Why choose quiet streets or bike lanes for active commuting?
questions.a: Lower traffic speed and volume reduce crash risk.

days.guide: Student writes a plan to replace two car trips weekly: routes, times, gear, safety, and weather plan.

questions.q: Name two benefits of active transportation.
questions.a: Adds daily physical activity; reduces emissions and traffic; saves money; improves mood.

weeks.assessment_key: Active commute plan rubric. 4 – Two specific trips with mapped routes, distances and times, safety plan (helmet, lights, route choice, signals), gear and weather backup, and estimated weekly activity minutes added. 3 (proficient) – Two trips with routes, safety, and timing. 2 – Vague trips or missing safety. 1 – Incomplete.

weeks.prep: Arrange pool access with a lifeguard (or plan the trail alternative). Review reach-throw-don't-go and rip-current escape. If the student is a weak swimmer, keep all water work in shallow water with an adult present.
misconceptions: Jumping in to save someone. Untrained rescuers often drown; reach with an object or throw a flotation device, and call for help.
Swimming straight toward shore against a rip current. Swim parallel to shore until out of the current, or float and signal for help.
Lifting the head forward to breathe in freestyle. Rotate the head to the side with one goggle in the water.

days.guide: Teach water safety: swim near lifeguards, never swim alone, reach-throw-don't-go, and rip currents (narrow channel flowing away from shore — swim parallel to escape).

questions.q: You're caught in a rip current. What do you do?
questions.a: Stay calm, don't fight it; swim parallel to the shore until out of the current, then angle back. If you can't, float and wave/yell for help.

questions.q: What does reach-throw-don't-go mean?
questions.a: Help a struggling swimmer by reaching with a pole/towel or throwing a flotation device from safety, rather than entering the water.

days.guide: Freestyle: horizontal body, flutter kick from hips, side breathing with body rotation. Backstroke: face up, ears in water, straight-arm recovery. (Alternative: stair intervals.)

questions.q: How should you breathe in freestyle?
questions.a: Exhale underwater, then rotate the head with the body to the side to inhale, keeping one ear in the water.

days.guide: Swim 20 minutes continuously (rest at wall as needed) or hike 60+ minutes. Record distance/HR.

questions.q: Why is swimming a good lifetime activity?
questions.a: It's low-impact, works the whole body, builds aerobic fitness, and is a survival skill.

days.guide: Practice treading water (eggbeater or scissor kick, sculling hands) and survival floating (back float) for time, in deep water only if competent with a lifeguard.

questions.q: Why is floating on your back useful in an emergency?
questions.a: It conserves energy while keeping your face out of the water, letting you breathe and wait for help.

days.guide: Give the outdoor pursuits quiz and review the unit log.

questions.q: Which way should a cyclist ride relative to traffic?
questions.a: In the same direction as traffic.

weeks.assessment_key: Outdoor pursuits quiz key: 1) Ten Essentials (any 8 correct). 2) Leave No Trace — pack out all trash. 3) Close contour lines = steep. 4) Back bearing of 45° = 225°. 5) ABC = Air, Brakes, Chain. 6) Ride with traffic. 7) Rip current: swim parallel to shore. 8) Reach-throw-don't-go. 9) Uphill hikers have right of way. Log: proficient = all unit activities logged with duration and intensity.

weeks.prep: Build a playlist with songs at different tempos (about 100–130 BPM). Find free dance-fitness videos (salsa/merengue basics, the Cupid Shuffle or Electric Slide). Clear floor space.
misconceptions: Counting music without finding the downbeat. Listen for the strong beat ('1'), often where a new phrase starts.
Thinking dance isn't real exercise. Heart-rate checks will show moderate-to-vigorous intensity.
Watching feet. Keep eyes up and posture tall; learn in slow motion first.

days.guide: Count songs in eights; clap the beat at different tempos. Teach grapevine, step-touch, box step, and V-step to 8-counts.

questions.q: How many counts does a grapevine to the right take?
questions.a: 4 counts: step right, cross left behind, step right, tap/touch left (then repeat left to complete 8).

days.guide: Teach basic salsa (forward-back basic, step on 1-2-3, pause 4, 5-6-7, pause 8) and merengue (march in place, step-together with hip action). Dance 20 minutes; check HR.

questions.q: In the salsa basic, which counts are paused?
questions.a: Counts 4 and 8 (steps on 1-2-3 and 5-6-7).

days.guide: Learn a full line dance from video; student teaches it to a family member using counts.

questions.q: How does a line dance repeat?
questions.a: It repeats the same sequence, usually turning to face a new wall each time.

days.guide: Student choreographs a 2-minute routine with at least six steps and two formations (e.g., line, circle) mapped to 8-counts on paper.

questions.q: What is choreography?
questions.a: The planned sequence of movements arranged to music.

days.guide: Perform for family; record HR before and after; reflect.

questions.q: HR rose from 80 to 150 after the routine. About what percent of estimated max is that for a 17-year-old?
questions.a: 150 ÷ 203 ≈ 74% of max — the upper end of moderate, bordering vigorous (CDC: moderate ≈ 64–76%, vigorous ≈ 77–93% of max). Compare with their Karvonen zones.

weeks.assessment_key: Choreography performance rubric. 4 – On-beat throughout, 6+ distinct steps, 2+ formations, smooth transitions, energetic, written 8-count map, HR data with reflection. 3 (proficient) – Mostly on-beat, 6 steps, 2 formations, HR recorded. 2 – Frequently off-beat or fewer steps. 1 – Incomplete.

weeks.prep: Set up 10 stations (cones, jump rope, bands, mats) with signs; interval timer app. Prepare a feedback survey (3–5 questions). Invite family or friends for Day 4.
misconceptions: Leading by talking constantly. Good instructors cue briefly, early, and specifically.
Offering only one level. Always give easier and harder modifications.
Thinking 40/20 means 'rest is optional.' Rest maintains quality and safety.

days.guide: Student completes a 10-station circuit, 40 s on/20 s off, and rates each station's RPE.

questions.q: How long is one round of a 10-station 40/20 circuit?
questions.a: 10 minutes (60 s per station × 10).

days.guide: Teach cueing: verbal ('chest up'), visual (demonstrate), tactile (only with permission, e.g., touch shoulder blade). Student cues a squat and a push-up.

questions.q: Give one verbal cue each for a squat and a push-up.
questions.a: Squat: 'Sit back, chest proud, knees out.' Push-up: 'Body like a plank, lower chest to fist height.'

days.guide: Student designs a 30-minute boot camp: 5-min warm-up, two circuits, cool-down, with easier/harder modifications for each exercise.

questions.q: Give an easier and harder modification for a push-up.
questions.a: Easier: incline or knee push-up. Harder: feet elevated or tempo/plyometric push-up.

days.guide: Student leads the class, adjusting for participants. Observe using the leadership rubric.

questions.q: A participant reports knee pain during lunges. What should the leader do?
questions.a: Stop the exercise for them and substitute a pain-free option (e.g., glute bridge or partial-range squat); recommend checking with a professional if pain persists.

days.guide: Distribute the survey; student summarizes results and writes a self-evaluation.

questions.q: Why collect participant feedback?
questions.a: To learn what worked and what to improve — leadership requires adapting to the group.

weeks.assessment_key: Leadership rubric. 4 – Clear plan with warm-up, 2 circuits, cool-down, modifications for every exercise; concise cues; adjusts in real time; safe environment; thoughtful self-evaluation using survey data. 3 (proficient) – Complete plan, clear cues, offers modifications, reflection. 2 – Missing modifications or unclear cues. 1 – Unsafe or unprepared.

weeks.prep: Gather a mat and a pillow or kick pad. Preview the techniques. Parental note: self-defense discussion may raise concerns about personal safety; keep it calm and empowering. Practice escapes slowly and gently with a trusted partner.
misconceptions: Believing strength is required. Technique and leverage (attacking the weak point, e.g., the thumb side of a grip) matter more.
Thinking self-defense is mainly fighting. Awareness, avoidance, and de-escalation come first; escaping and getting help is the goal.
Practicing at full speed. Use slow, controlled practice to avoid injury.

days.guide: Discuss situational awareness (head up, phone away, trust instincts) and de-escalation (calm voice, space, open hands). Role-play setting a firm boundary: 'Back off. I don't want to talk.'

questions.q: What is the primary goal of self-defense?
questions.a: To stay safe — avoid danger, de-escalate, escape, and get help.

days.guide: Teach a balanced fighting stance (feet staggered shoulder-width, hands up), palm-heel strike, and front kick into a pillow held by a partner.

questions.q: Why use a palm-heel strike rather than a closed fist?
questions.a: It is less likely to injure your own hand and is easier to deliver with force.

days.guide: Wrist-grab escape: rotate the wrist toward the attacker's thumb (weakest point) and pull out sharply. Bear-hug escape: drop weight low, create space, strike/step to escape. Slow practice only.

questions.q: Which direction do you pull to escape a one-hand wrist grab?
questions.a: Toward the gap between the grabber's thumb and fingers — the thumb side, the weakest point of the grip.

days.guide: Six rounds of 2-minute strike combos on the pad (palm strike, knee, front kick) with 1-minute rest.

questions.q: What fitness components does this pad workout train?
questions.a: Cardiorespiratory endurance, muscular endurance, power, and coordination.

days.guide: Student demonstrates techniques safely, then takes the unit quiz on dance and group fitness.

questions.q: How many beats are in a standard dance phrase count?
questions.a: 8 counts.

weeks.assessment_key: Technique demonstration (proficient): balanced stance with hands up; palm-heel strike with hip rotation; front kick with chamber; correct wrist-grab escape toward thumb; safe, controlled partner practice; verbal boundary statement. Quiz key: 1) Music counted in 8s. 2) Salsa pauses on 4 and 8. 3) Cueing types: verbal, visual, tactile. 4) Modifications let all levels participate safely. 5) 40/20 circuit = 40 s work, 20 s rest. 6) Self-defense priority: awareness/avoid/escape.

weeks.prep: Get a volleyball and a net or a rope tied between two posts at about 7'4"–7'11" (or lower for recreation). Find a smooth wall. Look up a 6-player rotation diagram.
misconceptions: Swinging arms in a forearm pass. Keep arms straight and together, angle the platform, and use the legs.
Setting with palms. Contact the ball with the finger pads in a triangle/diamond shape above the forehead.
Rotating counterclockwise. Teams rotate clockwise when they win back the serve.

days.guide: Teach the forearm pass: ready stance, hands joined, thumbs parallel, flat platform, contact on forearms, lift with legs. Wall pass goal: 30 in a row.

questions.q: Where on the arms should the ball contact in a forearm pass?
questions.a: On the flat part of the forearms just above the wrists, not the hands.

days.guide: Teach setting: hands form a window above the forehead, contact with finger pads, extend arms and legs. 50 self-sets.

questions.q: Why set with the fingertips instead of palms?
questions.a: It gives control and avoids a 'lift/carry' violation; palms cause slapping and poor accuracy.

days.guide: Practice underhand serve (step, swing from shoulder, contact the ball below center with heel of hand) and overhand float serve (toss, high elbow, firm contact). Serve to target zones.

questions.q: What makes an overhand float serve 'float'?
questions.a: Hitting it firmly with little or no spin, so it moves unpredictably in the air.

days.guide: Teach 6-player rotation (clockwise when gaining serve), pass-set-hit, three contacts maximum. Play modified games.

questions.q: How many contacts may a team use to return the ball?
questions.a: Three (a block does not count as one in indoor rules).

questions.q: When does a team rotate?
questions.a: When it wins the rally on the opponent's serve (side-out); players rotate one position clockwise.

days.guide: Skills test: 10 forearm passes and 10 sets to a target; 10 serves. Student diagrams a W serve-receive formation.

questions.q: What is a free ball?
questions.a: An easy, non-attacking return (usually a high pass) that the receiving team can easily set up for an attack.

weeks.assessment_key: Skills test: proficient = 6/10 passes and 6/10 sets to target zone, 7/10 legal serves. Diagram key: a W serve-receive shows 5 passers in a W shape (three across the middle/back, two front corners) with the setter near the net between right-front and middle, positions numbered 1–6 (1 = right back server, rotating clockwise).

weeks.prep: Get a flying disc (175 g ultimate disc), cones for end zones, and a field. Read USA Ultimate's Spirit of the Game summary. Look for local pickup games.
misconceptions: Running with the disc. The thrower must establish a pivot foot and has 10 seconds (stall count) to throw.
Contact defense. Ultimate is non-contact; marker must stay at least one disc-width away.
Thinking a referee is needed. Players call their own fouls and resolve disputes respectfully.

days.guide: Backhand (grip with thumb on top, step across, snap the wrist, flat release) and forehand/flick (two fingers under the rim, snap like skipping a stone). Throw at targets 10 and 20 yards.

questions.q: What causes a disc to flutter or wobble?
questions.a: Too little spin — a strong wrist snap creates spin that stabilizes the flight.

days.guide: Teach cuts: fake one way, explode the other; create space by clearing lanes. Practice give-and-go: pass, cut upfield, receive the return pass.

questions.q: What is a give-and-go?
questions.a: A player passes to a teammate and immediately cuts to receive a quick return pass.

days.guide: Compare person-to-person (each defender guards one player) and zone (defenders guard areas — useful in wind or against weaker throwers).

questions.q: When might a team choose zone defense?
questions.a: In windy conditions or against a team with poor long throws, to force many short passes and errors.

days.guide: Play ultimate with self-officiating. Review: score by catching in the end zone; turnover on drop, out-of-bounds, interception, or stall.

questions.q: Name three ways a turnover happens.
questions.a: Dropped or incomplete pass, interception/block, thrown out of bounds, or stall count reaches 10.

days.guide: Student writes an analysis of one offensive and one defensive strategy, using examples from play.

questions.q: What is Spirit of the Game?
questions.a: Ultimate's principle that players are responsible for fair play and rules adherence, respecting opponents and resolving calls without referees.

weeks.assessment_key: Strategy analysis rubric. 4 – Explains an offensive strategy (e.g., vertical stack, give-and-go) and a defensive strategy (person or zone) with how and why they work, cites specific game moments, evaluates effectiveness, and suggests improvement. 3 (proficient) – Accurately explains both with examples. 2 – Vague or partly inaccurate. 1 – Missing a strategy.

weeks.prep: Download the official rules of one sport (e.g., USA Volleyball or USA Pickleball) and a hand-signal chart. Get a whistle and a bracket template. Arrange a youth or family game to officiate.
misconceptions: Officials who hesitate lose control. Make calls clearly and promptly with correct signals.
Risk management is only first aid. It begins with prevention: inspecting space, equipment, and planning.
A bracket for 6 teams needs 6 slots. Use byes to fill to 8 in single elimination.
