days.guide: Student studies one sport's rules and practices 6+ hand signals (e.g., volleyball: point/side-out, ball in, ball out, net fault, double contact).

questions.q: In volleyball, what is the signal for 'ball out'?
questions.a: Both forearms raised vertically, palms facing the body (line judge flags up; referee raises forearms).

days.guide: Officiate a game using whistle and signals; keep score.

questions.q: Name two qualities of a good official.
questions.a: Knows the rules, is consistent, fair, decisive, communicates clearly, and remains calm.

days.guide: Walk a play area and identify hazards (uneven ground, glass, sprinklers, poles, sun/heat, no water). Write a checklist with prevention steps and an emergency plan (phone, first aid kit, address).

questions.q: Give three items for a risk-management checklist.
questions.a: Inspect surface and remove hazards; check equipment; have first aid kit, water, and phone; know address/emergency plan; warm-up planned.

days.guide: Plan a small tournament or fun run: bracket, schedule, roles, and safety plan.

questions.q: How many games are needed in a single-elimination bracket of 8 teams?
questions.a: 7 (each game eliminates one team; 8 − 1 = 7).

questions.q: How many byes for 6 teams in single elimination?
questions.a: 2 byes (to fill an 8-team bracket).

days.guide: Run or simulate the event; student reflects on leadership challenges.

questions.q: What should an event leader do if lightning or heat danger appears?
questions.a: Pause or cancel the event, move participants to safety, and follow the safety plan.

weeks.assessment_key: Event plan and officiating reflection rubric. 4 – Correct bracket (byes if needed), realistic schedule, roles, risk-management checklist with emergency plan, rules summary; reflection discusses specific calls, signals, and leadership problems with solutions. 3 (proficient) – Bracket, schedule, safety plan, and reflection on officiating. 2 – Missing safety plan or reflection lacks detail. 1 – Incomplete.

weeks.prep: Gather 5 food labels and print MyPlate guidelines (myplate.gov). Install a food-log app or use a notebook. Parental note: keep the focus on fueling performance, not weight; watch for signs of disordered eating.
misconceptions: Thinking carbohydrates are bad. Carbohydrates are the main fuel for moderate-to-intense exercise.
Believing more protein always means more muscle. Beyond needs, extra protein doesn't build more muscle; training does.
Using sports drinks for all workouts. Water is enough for most sessions under about an hour.

days.guide: Teach macronutrients: carbohydrate (4 kcal/g, main exercise fuel), protein (4 kcal/g, repair/build tissue), fat (9 kcal/g, long-duration fuel, vitamin absorption). Read five labels. Then a 30-minute workout.

questions.q: A snack has 20 g carbohydrate, 5 g protein, and 8 g fat. How many calories?
Which macronutrient is the main fuel for high-intensity exercise?
questions.a: Carbohydrate.

days.guide: Keep a 3-day food log; compare with MyPlate food groups (half the plate fruits and vegetables, grains with at least half whole, protein, dairy).

questions.q: What does MyPlate recommend filling half your plate with?
questions.a: Fruits and vegetables.

days.guide: Plan pre-workout (1–3 hours before, carb-rich, moderate protein, low fat/fiber) and post-workout (within about 1–2 hours, carbs + protein) snacks. Discuss hydration: drink regularly, monitor urine color (pale yellow); estimate needs. Then a tempo run.

questions.q: Give an example of a good post-workout snack.
questions.a: Chocolate milk, Greek yogurt with fruit, or a turkey sandwich — carbohydrate plus protein.

questions.q: What urine color suggests good hydration?
questions.a: Pale yellow (like lemonade).

days.guide: Student plans one day of meals for an active teen within a budget, using MyPlate groups.

questions.q: Name two budget-friendly protein sources.
questions.a: Beans/lentils, eggs, canned tuna, peanut butter, chicken thighs.

days.guide: Give the quiz and review the food-log analysis.

questions.q: How many calories per gram are in fat vs. carbohydrate?
questions.a: Fat 9 kcal/g; carbohydrate 4 kcal/g.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) Carbs 4, protein 4, fat 9 kcal/g. 2) Carbohydrate = primary fuel for intense exercise. 3) Protein = growth and repair. 4) Pre-workout meal 1–3 h before: carbs, moderate protein, low fat/fiber. 5) Recovery: carbs + protein. 6) Pale yellow urine = hydrated. 7) Half the plate fruits/vegetables. Food-log analysis rubric: proficient = 3 complete days, compared to MyPlate groups with specific gaps/strengths and two realistic changes.

weeks.prep: Prepare a sleep log (bedtime, wake time, quality 1–5). Find a short article on exercise and anxiety/mood (e.g., from the CDC or a major health organization). Gather a mat and foam roller if available.
misconceptions: Thinking rest days are lazy. Adaptation happens during recovery.
Believing more training is always better. Overtraining lowers performance and raises injury and illness risk.
Making up lost sleep only on weekends. Consistency in bedtime and wake time matters most.

days.guide: Start the sleep log; review recommendations (8–10 hours for ages 13–18). Do a 20–30 minute yoga session.

questions.q: How many hours of sleep do teens need?
questions.a: 8–10 hours per night (ages 13–18).

days.guide: Discuss overtraining signs (elevated resting HR, persistent fatigue/soreness, worsening performance, mood changes, frequent illness, poor sleep) and injury prevention. Active-recovery walk.

questions.q: List three signs of overtraining.
questions.a: Rising resting heart rate, persistent fatigue or soreness, declining performance, irritability, trouble sleeping, frequent illness.

days.guide: Read about exercise and anxiety; do 30 minutes of moderate cardio, rating mood before and after.

questions.q: How does exercise help mood?
questions.a: It releases endorphins and other neurotransmitters, reduces stress hormones over time, improves sleep, and gives a sense of accomplishment.

days.guide: Practice foam rolling, stretching, and breathing. Plan a weekly rest/active-recovery day.

questions.q: What is active recovery?
questions.a: Light, low-intensity activity (easy walk, swim, yoga) that promotes blood flow and recovery without adding stress.

days.guide: Student writes a recovery plan based on the sleep log (bedtime target, wind-down routine, rest day, signs to watch).

questions.q: What is one sleep-hygiene habit?
questions.a: Consistent sleep schedule, no screens 30–60 min before bed, cool dark quiet room, limiting caffeine after midday.

weeks.assessment_key: Recovery plan rubric. 4 – Uses the 7-day sleep log data (average hours), sets a bedtime meeting 8–10 h, specific sleep hygiene steps, weekly rest and active-recovery days, overtraining warning signs and responses, and stress strategies. 3 (proficient) – Data-based sleep target, hygiene steps, rest day, warning signs. 2 – General plan not tied to data. 1 – Incomplete.

weeks.prep: Collect three fitness product ads (online or magazines), and look up the FDA's dietary supplement page and your local parks & recreation website.
misconceptions: Assuming supplements are FDA-approved. The FDA does not approve dietary supplements for safety or effectiveness before they are sold.
Trusting testimonials and before/after photos as evidence. Look for peer-reviewed research and independent testing.
Believing wearables are perfectly accurate. Heart rate and calorie estimates can be off substantially, especially calories.

days.guide: Analyze three ads for red flags: 'quick results,' 'no effort,' 'spot reduction,' testimonials, 'secret' formulas, money-back pressure. Rate the evidence.

questions.q: Can you 'spot reduce' belly fat with ab exercises?
questions.a: No. Fat loss occurs throughout the body; ab exercises strengthen muscles but don't target fat in one area.

questions.q: Name three red flags in fitness ads.
questions.a: Promises of rapid results, 'no diet or exercise needed,' testimonials instead of research, 'miracle'/'secret' claims, spot reduction claims.

days.guide: Research the FDA's role (supplements are regulated as foods under DSHEA 1994; manufacturers are responsible for safety; FDA acts after problems arise). Evaluate one supplement (e.g., creatine, pre-workout) for evidence and risks; look for third-party testing seals (USP, NSF Certified for Sport).

questions.q: Does the FDA approve supplements before they are sold?
questions.a: No. Manufacturers are responsible for safety and labeling; the FDA can act against unsafe products after they're on the market.

questions.q: What does a USP or NSF Certified for Sport seal indicate?
questions.a: Independent testing that the product contains what the label says and is free of specified contaminants/banned substances — not that it is effective.

days.guide: Compare two free apps/wearables: test heart-rate accuracy against a manual pulse, step counts against counted steps, and usefulness.

questions.q: Your watch reads 150 bpm; your manual 15-second count is 34. What's the difference?
questions.a: Manual = 136 bpm; the watch is 14 bpm higher.

days.guide: Map free/low-cost community resources: parks, trails, rec centers, YMCA, school facilities, community classes.

questions.q: Name two low-cost options for staying active after high school.
questions.a: Public parks and trails, community recreation center classes, campus gyms, free online workout videos, pickup games.

days.guide: Student writes a consumer guide for teens: how to evaluate products, supplements, apps, and gyms.

questions.q: What question should you ask about any fitness product claim?
questions.a: What is the evidence — is it supported by independent, peer-reviewed research?

weeks.assessment_key: Consumer guide rubric. 4 – Explains red flags with examples, accurately describes FDA supplement regulation and third-party testing, compares apps with data, lists local resources, gives clear checklist. 3 (proficient) – Accurate red flags, FDA role, app comparison, local resources. 2 – Some inaccuracies (e.g., claims supplements are FDA-approved). 1 – Incomplete.

weeks.prep: Gather all year's fitness data (baseline, midyear, logs) and a plan template with FITT sections for cardio, strength, flexibility, and lifetime activities.
misconceptions: Making a plan too ambitious to follow. Adherence matters more than an ideal plan.
Leaving out flexibility or strength. A complete plan addresses all components.
Planning activities without considering access after high school (cost, location, schedule).

days.guide: Review data; student lists strengths and needs for each component.

questions.q: Why base a plan on personal data?
questions.a: So it targets actual needs and allows measurable progress (specificity and individualization).

days.guide: Write the cardio component with FITT; complete a cardio session.

questions.q: Give a FITT cardio plan meeting adult guidelines.
questions.a: Example: 4 days/week, moderate to vigorous (60–80% HRR), 30–45 minutes, running/cycling — at least 150 min moderate or 75 min vigorous weekly.

days.guide: Write strength and flexibility components; complete a strength session.

questions.q: How often should adults do muscle-strengthening activity?
questions.a: At least 2 days per week, working all major muscle groups.

days.guide: Choose two lifetime activities and plan access (location, cost, schedule, partners).

questions.q: What makes an activity 'lifetime'?
questions.a: It can be done across the lifespan with few people, modest equipment, and is enjoyable (e.g., hiking, swimming, pickleball, cycling).

days.guide: Review the draft against the rubric and give feedback.

questions.q: What does 'adherence' mean in fitness?
questions.a: Sticking to the plan consistently over time.

weeks.assessment_key: Fitness plan draft rubric. 4 – Based on year data; FITT for cardio, strength, flexibility; meets guidelines; two lifetime activities with access plans; SMART goals; progression and self-monitoring method. 3 (proficient) – All components with FITT, lifetime activities, goals. 2 – Missing a component or FITT details. 1 – Incomplete.

weeks.prep: Have the fitness journal and written plan ready; heart-rate app or stopwatch. Check access for the lifetime activity.
misconceptions: Not logging because the session 'felt normal.' Self-monitoring keeps the plan honest.
Changing many variables at once. Adjust one variable at a time to know what works.
Ignoring enjoyment. Enjoyment strongly predicts long-term adherence.

days.guide: Complete the plan's cardio workout; log average HR and RPE.

questions.q: Your average HR was 158 and your 60–80% zone is 150–177. Were you in zone?
questions.a: Yes, 158 falls within 150–177.

days.guide: Complete the strength workout; log sets, reps, loads.

questions.q: Why log loads for each exercise?
questions.a: To track progressive overload and know when to increase.

days.guide: Spend 45 minutes on a chosen lifetime activity; log duration and enjoyment (1–10).

questions.q: Why rate enjoyment?
questions.a: Enjoyable activities are more likely to be continued (adherence).

days.guide: 20-minute flexibility/yoga routine; note tight areas.

questions.q: How often should flexibility work be done?
questions.a: At least 2–3 days per week; daily is beneficial.

days.guide: Compare logs to the plan, identify one adjustment, and revise.

questions.q: Your RPE in every cardio session was 3. What adjustment fits the FITT principle?
questions.a: Increase intensity (pace or intervals) or time, applying overload gradually.

weeks.assessment_key: Plan implementation log rubric. 4 – All 5 sessions logged with required data (HR, RPE, sets/reps/loads, duration, enjoyment, tight areas), honest comparison to plan, one well-justified adjustment written into the revised plan. 3 (proficient) – Complete log, comparison, and one adjustment. 2 – Missing sessions or adjustment. 1 – Incomplete.

weeks.prep: Gather stopwatch, measuring tape, sit-and-reach box, baseline and midyear data. Use the same routes and protocols. Schedule tests after a rest day.
misconceptions: Expecting improvement in every test. Maintenance in some components is also success.
Comparing to classmates. Compare to your own past results and HFZ.
Ignoring test conditions. Note weather, sleep, and illness.

days.guide: Mile run/walk and resting HR, same protocol as before.

questions.q: Mile: 10:40 baseline, 9:52 midyear, 9:20 final. Total improvement?
questions.a: 80 seconds (1:20) faster than baseline.

days.guide: Push-ups, curl-ups (cadence), plank hold.

questions.q: Why is the plank a measure of muscular endurance rather than strength?
questions.a: It measures how long muscles can sustain a contraction, not maximal force.

days.guide: Sit-and-reach (both sides) and shoulder stretch.

questions.q: What adult activity guideline should a 5-year plan meet?
questions.a: At least 150 minutes moderate (or 75 vigorous) aerobic activity per week, plus muscle strengthening 2+ days per week.

days.guide: List barriers (schedule, cost, location, motivation) with specific strategies and community resources.

questions.q: Barrier: no gym at new job location. Strategy?
questions.a: Bodyweight/band workouts at home, run or walk outdoors, find a community rec center or campus gym.

days.guide: Student plans and leads a 40-minute family workout: warm-up, cardio, strength, flexibility, cool-down.

questions.q: What order should a balanced session follow?
questions.a: Warm-up → main cardio/strength work → cool-down with flexibility.

days.guide: Student presents the 5-year plan with data in a 5-minute talk.

questions.q: What makes a fitness data presentation persuasive?
questions.a: Clear graphs showing change, explanation of causes, and specific goals tied to the data.

days.guide: 400-word reflection on how attitudes toward fitness changed.

questions.q: What is one habit-building strategy?
questions.a: Schedule workouts at a consistent time, start small, track progress, and pair activity with enjoyment or a partner.
